scenes.narration: Watch these four pieces. Slide them into a new arrangement, and a square hole appears. Nothing was removed. Nothing was stretched. So where did that extra space come from? Both arrangements seem to make the same big triangle: thirteen units across and five units high. But that word, triangle, is the trap. Look closely at the two sloping pieces. One rises three units while running eight across. The other rises two while running five. Those slopes are three eighths and two fifths. They are close, but they are not equal. So their slanted edges cannot form one straight line. In the first arrangement, the outline bends slightly inward. In the second, it bends slightly outward. Let us compare both outlines against a true straight diagonal. This lower view magnifies only the vertical deviation, twelve times, so the tiny difference becomes visible. The thin region between the two outlines has exactly one square unit of area. That is the space now occupied by the hole. The pieces always cover thirty two square units. The second outline encloses thirty three, including the empty square. No area was created. We changed the boundary while letting our eyes assume it stayed the same. Watch the pieces return. The hole closes as the outline bends back inward. Next time a rearrangement seems impossible, check the edge you assumed was straight.
